## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kapijātaka* (Ja 250), translated as "The Monkey", is a narrative preserved in the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon [SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional framing preserved on SuttaCentral, the Buddha delivered the story while residing at the Jetavana monastery near Sāvatthī, taking occasion from the behavior of a hypocritical monk [SuttaCentral]. The story opens with the verse theme beginning "A holy sage" [SuttaCentral].

Computational text-reuse data from DharmaNexus identifies five matching Pali passages shared internally with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (*Dutiyo bhāgo*), with the longest segment spanning §0.4–2.1 of the text against §1754_9–1758_0 of the commentary [DharmaNexus]. Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies any cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan traditions [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four modern translations across four languages [SuttaCentral]. The secondary literature and edition excerpts identified in reference searches do not treat Ja 250 directly, instead addressing other homonymous or related monkey birth-stories, specifically the *Kapijātaka* (Ja 404) and various versions of the *Mahākapijātaka* (such as Ja 407 and Ja 516).
